Three things. Keep your routine. Routine is key. When you stop working you lose a routine and without one it's so easy for your time to get away from you. So get up at the same time every day, each meals at the same time. Look for a job at the same time.

Two, finding a job is now your job. And like any job it's got long regular hours five days a week. Mon-Fri, you should be looking for a job for 4-8 hours a day. It doesn't even matter if you want the job you apply for. Applying is good practice. You need interviews.

Three, your resume is not good enough. Even if you think it's good enough, it's not. Have it professionally checked. Resume standards change almost yearly as to what people are looking for. Computers scan resumes looking for keywords. You need to have those keywords in a resume.

I learned these three steps in a job class offered by my county after being unemployed for 2 years. One week after the month long class, I had a job. A year after the class I was off social assistance. Two years after the class I had a new better job. Three years, I am now in a stable career with benefits and a future. It gets better. Dont' give up. I will reply to any questions you may have. Good luck.

I have been taught these things as well, so it's good to know that they work. I've got a routine, my number priority is job hunting, but I'm probably lacking in the keyword department. I'm happy that things worked out for you. I'll get my resume re-reviewed as suggested.

Getting rejected isn't failing. You're going to get rejected a lot.

But, if you've been looking for awhile, there are a few things you could try.

  1. Apply to everything. Try looking in other fields. Apply to things you don't think your qualified for. Apply to things you think you're overqualified for. Don't artificially limit your search.

  2. Train for certifications. Find out what things are relative to the work you are looking for. You can find online resources for pretty much any certification, and many only require you to take a single test to certify. These will help a lot on a resume if you don't have any other education to flaunt.

  3. Get a professional to review your resume. This one is pretty self-explanatory. You don't want your resume to look like crap.

Those are all aimed at finding work in the near future. On the other hand, if you don't necessarily need the money and have a lot of time to invest, you could go/go back to school.

If money isn't the deciding factor, this is an excellent opportunity to take your career in whatever direction you choose. Find out what you want to do. Find out what skills or knowledge you need to do it. Gain the skills. Then do it.

I tend to switch career fields every six or seven years, so that's meant plenty of time being unemployed. I have far too much experience in this.

It's easy to fall into the cycle of depression. You have no income, no hope. You wake up only because there's nothing else to do, and before you know it, the whole day was wasted. I've gotten to the point of not even changing for days at a time.

What's going to save you is setting a schedule that you're going to take just as seriously as a job...only you're the boss, so there's no calling in sick. Set that alarm, and join the rat race on weekdays. Write it down, so you have no choice. I would use a whiteboard in my office to keep focused. Start off with an hour of exercise. You said you moved south from the north east. That means it's beautiful out there in the morning. Spend an hour jogging or bike riding. No excuses. Every day. Next you need to give yourself two hours of applying for jobs, and making telephone calls. No web surfing, no distractions. This is your job. You should have a lunch hour on your agenda, so everything can wait on that. Remember, you need to follow up with every place you put in a resume. Make calls. Ask to set up an interview. Don't be afraid of being pushy. After lunch, spend an hour cleaning the house and getting dinner ready. I know this made me a great cook during my unemployment period. After that hour, it's another two hours of applying.

Next, you need to find ways to network. Honest truth in today's economy is that your ability to get hired depends on who you know as much as what you know. What field are you interested in? I can promise you that there's a professional meet up of people int hat profession who will open doors for you. Budget enough to afford a cup of coffee for each of these meetings.

It's a full and busy day if you do it right, but that kind of focus will help you mentally (and physically with the five hours of exercise each week). Then when the weekend hits, you can just sit back and enjoy it.
